note.text: A transitive use takes a direct object: Bih opened the box. An intransitive use has no direct object: the box opened. A verb can allow both patterns, so classify the use in the sentence rather than attaching one permanent label to every spelling. A place or time phrase is not automatically a direct object. Linking complements also need a different analysis: happy in she seems happy describes the subject rather than naming an object acted on.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify a direct object and distinguish transitive from intransitive uses in context. Builds on: word functions and finite clause patterns. Leads to: adverbials, clause structure and accurate sentence construction.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: A transitive use takes a direct object: Bih opened the box. An intransitive use has no direct object: the box opened. A verb can allow both patterns, so classify the use in the sentence rather than attaching one permanent label to every spelling. A place or time phrase is not automatically a direct object. Linking complements also need a different analysis: happy in she seems happy describes the subject rather than naming an object acted on.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original pairs: Ayuk writes a report; Ayuk writes after supper. The report is a direct object in the first use. After supper gives time in the second. Bih opened the door; the door opened. The change affects the pattern even though the verb is the same. Do not insert an object into arrive merely because another verb accepts one.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Find the verb use, then ask whether a noun phrase functions as its direct object. Distinguish object from an adverbial phrase or subject complement. Test the complete clause and its meaning instead of counting how many words follow the verb.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: transitive use: a verb use taking a direct object.
intransitive use: a verb use without a direct object.
adverbial phrase: a phrase giving circumstances such as time or place.
subject complement: an expression describing or identifying the subject after a linking verb.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: Bih opened the box; consider the verb’s relation to the box.
The box opened; no direct object follows opened.
Ayuk writes after supper; after supper gives time.
Bih seems happy; happy describes Bih.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Any word after a verb must be its direct object. Correction: A direct object has a grammatical role, not merely a position after a verb.
A verb with no direct object can never form a complete clause. Correction: An intransitive use can be complete without a direct object.
After supper is necessarily the direct object of writes. Correction: The phrase states when, rather than what is written.
Happy is always a direct object receiving an action in seems happy. Correction: The linking pattern relates the description to the subject.

w: transitive use with after lunch as object

Arrived is the verb.
It is not the naming expression.
The door is the subject here.
